There is no final value. Either output scrolls forever (BadHellos with `i > 3`) or nothing happens and the program 'hangs'. Over a very long run, int overflow may eventually make the test false (BadHellos stops after about 2^31 lines).
Each pass leaves the condition's variables either unchanged or moving away from false (i grows while the test is `i > 3`). So the state after the pass satisfies the condition again.

A loop is finite only if its update moves the control variable towards making the condition false. Wrong direction (`i--` with `i < n`), wrong step (`i += 0` or `x += 0.5` on an int), or a condition that the update can step over (`i != 10` with `i += 3`) all give infinite loops.

items.text: Naming convention: a style rule (not a language rule) for choosing identifiers. Variables and methods use lowerCamelCase, classes UpperCamelCase, constants UPPER_CASE_WITH_UNDERSCORES, and names describe meaning.

Variable names begin with a lowercase letter and capitalize each later word (firstName). Class names begin with a capital. Constants are all uppercase with _ between words. Names should indicate what the variable means.
Conventions have no execution order: the compiler checks only that an identifier is legal and declared, never whether it follows convention.
A program's output does not depend on its names: renaming total to t everywhere gives identical results.
Following or breaking a convention changes no state; it only changes how readable the code is.
Each variable's name should describe what it holds (count, sum, maxSoFar). Single letters suit only short-lived loop indices.
Constants are written in ALL_CAPS with underscores, which sets them apart from lowerCamelCase variables and signals that they never change.
Good names make each variable's role visible (sum for a gatherer, count for a counter, max for a most-wanted holder, i for a stepper), so a reader can recognize the plan without tracing.

Renaming consistently keeps the program's meaning, because what it computes does not depend on names. A misleading name (max holding a minimum) still compiles and runs the same, but readers draw wrong conclusions.
Apply the conventions to every name you write. Short names fit only tiny scopes (loop index i, coordinates x and y). No naming convention can replace the code that actually computes the value.

rule broken: A name does not compute or guarantee a value. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Trusting a descriptive name instead of the code (e.g. assuming average holds the mean although it was never divided): wrong output that the name hides.

items.text: Identity: a two-dimensional array, an array of arrays used to represent a table or matrix with M rows and N columns.
Declarative: declare double[][] a; create with new double[M][N] (rows first, then columns); refer to row i, column j as a[i][j]. Entries start at 0 (numbers) or false (boolean).
Sequencing: new double[M][N] creates an array of M references and then M row arrays of N defaults. a[i][j] evaluates a[i] (checked against a.length = M) and then [j] (checked against a[i].length).
Result: a[i][j] has the element type; a.length is the number of rows M; a[i].length is the length of row i; a[i] is a double[] row.
State transition: a[i][j] = v changes one element of row i; a[i] = new double[K] replaces the whole row i with a new array; other rows are untouched.
The transition matrix is a 2-D double array p[i][j] with one row per page; each row holds a probability distribution.
A 2-D array uses two indices, and the first chooses the row array: a[i][j] is (a[i])[j].
Since each row is a separate array, rows may have different lengths; such arrays are ragged.
Matrix operations index a[i][j] in nested loops (two for addition, three for multiplication).
The same notation extends to any number of dimensions: a[i][j][k] for double[][][].
Row-major order visits a[i][j] with the outer loop over rows i; column-major puts the loop over j outside.
Plan/role: store tables, matrices, grids and images indexed by row and column (grades by student and test, lattice intersections, pixels).
Conservation: swapping the loop order for an element-wise operation keeps the result but changes the processing order. Swapping the indices (a[j][i]) transposes and goes out of bounds when M != N.

Applicability: use a 2-D array for data naturally indexed by two integers (rows by columns). Use a ragged array when rows differ, a 1-D array when one index suffices, and higher dimensions for 3-D models.

rule broken: Indices must be within each dimension (i < a.length, j < a[i].length). Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: row and column bounds swapped in a non-square M-by-N array, or j bounded by N on a shorter ragged row (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException)

Definite assignment: the compile-time rule that a local variable must certainly have been assigned before any read of it.

Every access of a local variable must be preceded by an assignment on every possible path, or the program does not compile. The analysis ignores run-time values, except for constant booleans and the operators && || ?:.

The compiler walks the control flow. After a declaration with no initializer the variable is unassigned, and an assignment makes it assigned on that path. Where paths merge (after if/else) it counts as assigned only if every incoming path assigned it, and an assignment inside a while body does not count after the loop.
The result appears at compile time: the code either compiles or reports 'variable x might not have been initialized'. No default value is ever produced for a local variable.
The first assignment (initialization) moves a variable from unassigned to holding a value, and only then may it be read.

The rule guarantees that no program reads a meaningless value. The matching plan is to initialize counters and accumulators before the loop that updates them (int sum = 0; then sum += i inside the loop).

items.text: The while statement is a loop (iteration statement): it repeats a body as long as a boolean condition is true.

Syntax: while (<boolean expression>) { <statements> } (braces optional for one statement). Meaning: if the expression is false do nothing; if true, execute the body, then check the expression again, and continue as long as it is true.
1. Evaluate the condition. 2. If false, skip the body and continue after the loop. 3. If true, execute the whole body, then go back to step 1.
A while statement has no value; its result is the state and output after the passes it made: e.g. TenHellos with i = 4 and i <= 10 prints 4th to 10th Hello (7 passes) and leaves i = 11.

One pass: test the condition with the current values, then (if true) apply every body statement once in order; the variables assigned in the body change and nothing else; a false test ends the loop with the state unchanged.
The loop condition is a boolean expression evaluated before every pass; the loop stops the first time it is false, so the body must eventually make it false.
do { body } while (c); means the same as while (c) { body } except that the first test is omitted, so the body runs at least once.
break exits the loop immediately, so a while loop can end either by a false test or by a break; while (true) needs a break (or is infinite).
An animation repeats clear/draw/show/pause steps inside a loop, typically one that runs indefinitely.
A convergence test is the while condition that keeps refining an estimate until the error is within tolerance, e.g. while (Math.abs(t - c/t) > epsilon * t).
The body is the block that the while repeats; it runs only after a true test and is completed before the next test.
The while condition usually tests a loop variable that is initialized before the loop and updated in the body; if the body never changes it, the loop never ends.
To trust a while loop, state what stays true on every pass and why the condition eventually becomes false (e.g. v is always a power of 2, v increases, so the loop terminates).
Binary conversion uses while loops: one to find the largest power of 2 <= N, and one to cast out powers of 2 in decreasing order.
if and while have the same form, but if tests its condition once and runs the block at most once, while while tests again after every pass and repeats the block as long as the condition is true.

double is a primitive data type: Java's 64-bit IEEE 754 floating-point type for representing real numbers.

Values are 64-bit IEEE 754 numbers (about 15 significant digits) plus the special values Infinity and NaN; +, -, *, / (and %) are defined; if at least one operand of a binary arithmetic operator is double, the operation is a floating-point operation.

Operators are applied in precedence order, left operand first; at each operator, if one operand is double the other is widened to double before the operation, and the result is rounded to the nearest double before the next operator uses it.
The result has type double: 5.0/3.0 is 1.6666666666666667, 10/3.0 is 3.3333333333333335, 1.0/0.0 is Infinity, Math.sqrt(-1.0) is NaN; println always shows a decimal part (3.0, not 3).

An assignment to a double variable stores the nearest representable value (x = x + 0.1 replaces x with the rounded sum); no double operation throws an exception, so the variable may end up holding Infinity or NaN.

Type flow decides the division: with two int operands a / b discards the fraction (10/3 is 3, and double d = 10/3; stores 3.0); if either operand is double the other is promoted and the fraction is kept (10/3.0 is 3.3333333333333335).
